query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Switching from high‐thermal‐load laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of AlCrFeNiSi powders to a near‐room‐temperature 3D ink‐extrusion printing process followed by low‐temperature sintering with in situ silicide coating will reduce residual stresses, preserve or enhance mechanical properties, and simplify processing for miniature components.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional atomized AlCrFeNiSi feedstock powder produced by gas atomization with typical particle size distribution suited for LPBF.
generation.intervention: Employ a low‐thermal‐input additive approach by printing the feedstock as a powder–loaded ink at room temperature, then consolidating the green parts via a controlled sintering step (600–800 °C) that favors diffusion and neck growth without inducing high thermal gradients, and finally applying a silicide coating (via in situ pack cementation) to enhance surface integrity.
generation.conditions: Processing window: Room‐temperature ink‐extrusion printing with layer thicknesses of 20–50 µm, followed by sintering at 600–800 °C for densification, targeting miniature components (dimensions typically <10 mm) under ambient atmosphere. Testing to be performed at room temperature for residual stress (e.g., via XRD), microstructural integrity (SEM/TEM) and mechanical properties (micro-tensile, hardness).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a homogeneous and fine‐grained microstructure with minimized thermal gradients, aided by the subsequent silicide coating which acts as a diffusion barrier and stress relaxer.
generation.mechanism: By drastically reducing the thermal cycles during manufacturing (i.e. printing at room temperature rather than melting), the process minimizes residual stresses and microstructural defects that normally arise from rapid solidification in LPBF. The controlled sintering allows consolidation without high temperature induced degradation, while the silicide coating further stabilizes surface phases and mitigates any oxidation, leading to improved mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to components produced by conventional high‐energy LPBF, the printed and sintered components with silicide coating are expected to exhibit significantly lower residual stresses, better preserved ductility and tensile strength, and a simplified, more robust processing route, all of which translate to enhanced performance for miniature structural applications.
generation.baseline: LPBF‐produced miniature components that are subject to high residual thermal stresses, micro‐cracking, and degraded mechanical properties due to rapid melting and solidification.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for miniature components manufactured from AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock with similar particle size distributions; applicability to larger scales or different alloy compositions may require further adjustment of the sintering and coating parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal sintering temperature and duration, as well as the precise coating thickness necessary to achieve the desired mechanical and oxidation resistance properties, will require fine‐tuning. Additionally, potential differences in densification kinetics in the ink–extrusion process versus LPBF may lead to variability in outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of miniature components using identical AlCrFeNiSi feedstock. One set will be fabricated using conventional high–thermal–load LPBF processing, while the other will be produced via the proposed room–temperature ink–extrusion printing followed by sintering (600–800 °C) and subsequent in situ silicide coating. Ensure all other variables (e.g., powder composition, particle size) are held constant.
measurements: Residual stress analysis via X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Microstructural characterization using scanning/transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM)
Mechanical testing including micro–tensile tests and hardness measurements at room temperature
Oxidation and corrosion resistance testing under controlled environments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the components produced by the low–thermal–load process do not show a statistically significant reduction in residual stresses and an improvement in mechanical properties (or if the silicide coating does not form effectively to improve surface stability) relative to the LPBF–produced baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations. Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.
